newsitem.title: USA: Pa. utility reform bill to benefit bondholders.
newsitem.headline: Pa. utility reform bill to benefit bondholders.

text.p: Legislation to deregulate the electric utility industry in Pennsylvania may result in significant gains for bondholders if approved by the state's legislature, according to several Wall Street analysts.

Pennsylvania Governor Tom Ridge is pushing to pass the legislation by November 27, the last day of the current legislative session. A spokesman for Ridge says the bill is supported by both utility and consumer groups.
"Time is our only problem," said a spokesman for the governor. "We have a shot because this is a consensus bill."
CURRENT UTILITY BONDHOLDERS STAND TO GAIN

Wall Street traders note that when similar stranded cost legislation was passsed in California, outstanding bonds from utilities in that state tightened by three- to five-basis points immediately thereafter.

Merrill Lynch and Co Inc utilities analyst Leo Kelser said that if the Pennsylvania legislation is passed, the same is likely to happen to the bonds of two utilities in the state which have the highest amount of stranded asset costs: PECO Energy and Duquesne Light.
Kelser said the bonds have already tightened by several basis points on news that the legislation has been drafted.
"We still have the potential for more spread tightening ... at least a couple of basis points relative to other utilities if the legslation is passed," said Kelser.
He added, "As other states jump on the bandwagon, there is the potential for the whole electric utility sector to tighten at least several basis points on top of that."
New York, New Jersey and Illinois are expected to deal with the issue of stranded costs in the near future, he said.
RATING UPGRADES EXPECTED
Merrill's Kelser said spread tightening among utility bonds will be driven by an improvement in the fundamental and technical outlook for utilities as a result of the legislation.
Richard Cortright, director at Standard & Poor's, confirmed rating upgrades are possible as companies use the proceeds of securitization offerings to deleverage their balance sheets.

"Any securitization of this nature is pretty positive from a credit quality point of view. Removing these assets from a balance sheet which otherwise are not likely to be recovered is clearly a good thing," he said.

From a technical standpoint, Kelser said current investors in utility paper will benefit if the utilities use the proceeds raised from securitization to repurchase outstanding debt, potentially at a premium.
"Our expectation is for utilities to use a significant portion of the proceeds from these asset-backed transactions to retire existing on-balance-sheet debt," he said.
A spokesman for PECO confirmed that the utility plans to use part of the proceeds from securitization to pay down higher-cost debt. Calls to Duquesne were not returned.
RECOUPING STRANDED ASSET COSTS
If the bill is passed, Pennsylvania will become the second state in the country, after California, to deal with issues surrounding the transition of electric utilities to a deregulated environment.

From a bondholder's perspective, one of the most important parts of the bill is a provision that allows Pennsylvania utilities to recoup their stranded costs by levying a surcharge on electricity consumers. Stranded costs are those that could not be recovered in a deregulated environment.
A similar provision was included in the California legislation which was passed in September.

"This has huge significance," says Terran Miller, utilities analyst at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "Stranded assets have been a huge concern for high-cost utilities who worry that when competition arrives, they will not be able to recover their sunken investments in nuclear plants and other assets that are now above market costs."

To recoup the costs, the legislation will allow the utilities to issue asset-backed securities (ABS), known as "rate reduction," or "transition" bonds, backed by the revenues generated from the consumer surcharges.

Analysts explained that securitization financing will allow the utilities to raise money at relatively cheap rates. The savings will flow back to consumers in the form of consumer rate reductions, which utilities are mandated to enact in the legislation, they added.
"The whole concept of asset-securitization offers a way out for high-cost utilities, while at the same time giving some benefit to consumers. It's a win-win situation for all parties," says Miller.
NEW OPPORTUNITIES FOR ABS INVESTORS

Ellen Lapson, head of investor-owned electric utility ratings at Fitch Investors Service, said the new market for ABS backed by stranded asset surcharges could ultimately grow to $40 billion, assuming certain tax issues are favorably resolved.
Wall Street experts predicted the securities are likely to be marketed to traditional ABS investors, who will be most familiar with their non-recourse status and likely cash-flow characteristics.

"This will be a fairly standard securitization deal. What makes it unique is that you are securitizing a legislative promise to pay, rather than a receivable in which a consumer promises to pay," said an investment banker who is working on one of the first deals for a California utility.

Wall Street sources said the first transactions from California utilities are likely to hit the market by the end of next year. Pacific Gas and Electric Co has hired Morgan Stanely & Co, and Southern California Edison Co has hired Salomon Brothers Inc as advisors. Sources said it is still uncertain who will underwrite the transactions.

The California legislation provides for up to $5.0 billion of ABS to be issued by electric utilities in the state. Sources said under the Pennsylvania legislation, the state's public utility commission is likely to decide on the appropriate amount.
RISKS FOR ABS INVESTORS
Rating agency analysts said that while the new securities will represent extremely safe investments, they will also have some unique risks.

S&P's Cortright said the longer the period in which the surcharges are collected, the greater the potential risks to investors. "To the extent these amounts are recoverable, they should be recovered quickly. We are particularly concerned about political pressures over the long-term."
Fitch's Lapson pointed out investors must also consider the risk that over time new technologies may be developed that would siphon off usage from wire-distributed electric utilities.
"This is not a major problem if the time frame is within five- to 10-years, but it will be more of a problem during a longer period," she said.
